title: Cotton tree (wawuburra) and the kapok bushes

names.gloss: cottontree. Canoes were made out of these and the candlenut tree, bilar. When it blooms (big red flowers) it signals the start of the scrub hen egg season

scientificName: Bombax ceiba var. leiocarpum; also Cochlospermum and Gossypium australe

identification.basis: The dictionary's cotton tree has 'big red flowers' and was a canoe timber; Anderson's Bloomfield canoe timber was 'a cotton tree (probably Bombax malabaricum)', the old name of Bombax ceiba, and Roth's Endeavour River canoe tree was the same. The kapok bushes (Cochlospermum) and native cotton (Gossypium) near Karma Waters are different plants given here for comparison.

summary: **[wawuburra](word:wawuburra)** is the cotton tree, and the dictionary gives it two jobs: 'Canoes were made out of these and the candlenut tree, *bilar*. When it blooms (big red flowers) it signals the start of the scrub hen egg season' [ref:hershberger1982]. It is the red silk-cotton tree, *Bombax ceiba*, a tall straight tree of the monsoon forest and river banks that drops every leaf in the dry and then covers itself in cup-shaped red flowers, 'when most other forms of vegetation in the community are looking rather drab and forlorn', before splitting its capsules to let out the cream kapok [ref:rfk-bombax] [ref:wiki-bombax]. Its cousins are the kapok bush *Cochlospermum*, which flowers yellow on bare rocky ridges in the dry and whose roots Palmer saw roasted on the Mitchell in 1883, and the native cotton *Gossypium australe* of sandy ground [ref:rfk-cochlospermum] [ref:palmer1883] [ref:wiki-gossypium].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body: **[wawuburra](word:wawuburra)** 'cottontree' [ref:hershberger1982]. Its partners in the dictionary: **[bilar](word:bilar)**, the [candlenut](entry:candlenut), the other canoe tree; and **[ngakun](word:ngakun)**, the flame tree, which also 'signals the time when the scrub hen eggs are in season' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Endeavour River (Guugu Yimithirr) name for the *Bombax* was *nanggarbura* [ref:roth1910]. Palmer's Mitchell River name for the kapok bush was *Kurrutcha*, from a language he does not name [ref:palmer1883]. The dictionary has no separate word on record for the kapok bush or for native cotton.

sections.heading: The tree, and its cousins
sections.body:
**The cotton tree**, *Bombax ceiba* var. *leiocarpum*, the 'northern cottonwood' or 'red silk-cotton tree'. 'This Asian tropical tree has a straight tall trunk and its leaves are deciduous in winter. Red flowers with 5 petals appear in the spring before the new foliage. It produces a capsule which, when ripe, contains white fibres like cotton' [ref:wiki-bombax]. It grows to about 20 m; 'the trunk and limb bear numerous conical spines particularly when young, but get eroded when older'; the leaves are palmate, five or six leaflets from one point on a long stalk [ref:wiki-bombax]. The flowers are 'usually produced when the tree is leafless', with a corolla 6–8 cm long, densely hairy outside, the stamens fused into a central column; the capsules, about 10 cm, are 'densely packed with large quantities of cream fibrous material which resembles cotton wool and surrounds the seed, but is not really attached to the seed' [ref:rfk-bombax]. In Australia it is 'widespread in WA, NT, CYP and NEQ', from sea level to about 300 m, 'usually grows in monsoon forest' and along rivers; 'flowers are produced in the dry season when the tree is completely leafless' [ref:rfk-bombax]. The kapok is an 'inferior grade' of the commercial fibre, and the tree is the food plant of the common aeroplane butterfly's caterpillars [ref:rfk-bombax].

**The kapok bushes**, *Cochlospermum*. The one in the rainforest key, *C. gillivraei*, is 'usually a small, short-boled tree', deciduous and 'leafless for a period between July and October', with deeply lobed leaves 'radiating like the blades of a windmill', flowers 7–10 cm across 'usually produced when the tree is leafless', petals marked inside with pink-red spots, and inflated capsules 6–9.5 cm long that fall apart at maturity to let out the silky seed hairs; it 'usually grows in rocky situations in open forest' and 'adds a considerable amount of colour to an environment which is often bereft of colour or green leaves' [ref:rfk-cochlospermum]. Palmer's *Kurrutcha* of the Mitchell, 'a peculiar thorny tree, with large palmatifid leaf, growing in a cluster or crown near the top', with a spiny stem, 10 to 12 feet high 'on the banks of the Mitchell in good soil', with a disagreeable smell, is named by him as a *Cochlospermum*, though his spiny stem and river-bank habit read like the cotton tree itself; either way, 'the roots of the young trees, which are long and thick, are roasted, when the skin peels off, leaving the edible part white and delicate and well-flavoured' [ref:palmer1883].

**Native cotton**, *Gossypium australe*, 'an endemic woody shrub, related to cotton', across northern Australia, grows on sandy ground near watercourses; it is a true cotton, with a small boll of lint [ref:wiki-gossypium].

sections.heading: Cotton tree, kapok bush, flame tree
sections.body:
- **Cotton tree** (*Bombax*): a tall tree, spiny when young, red flowers on bare branches, big kapok capsules; river and monsoon forest [ref:rfk-bombax] [ref:wiki-bombax].
- **Kapok bush** (*Cochlospermum*): a small crooked tree of the rocky ridges, yellow flowers on bare branches, windmill leaves, kapok capsules [ref:rfk-cochlospermum].
- **Flame tree** (*ngakun*), the dictionary's other egg-season tree, which also flowers red on bare wood; the dictionary gives it a yam's name too [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Native cotton** (*Gossypium*): a shrub, not a tree, grey-leaved, with a pink hibiscus flower and a small cotton boll [ref:wiki-gossypium].
- **Coral tree** (*Erythrina*): King's 1819 canoe timber at the Bloomfield, another soft-wooded, spiny, red-flowered tree of the coast, and the shield wood of the Mitchell [ref:king1827] [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Signs
sections.body:
- **Red flowers on a leafless tree** by a coastal river in the dry: the cotton tree, and the start of the [scrub-hen](entry:scrub-hen) egg season [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:rfk-bombax].
- **Yellow flowers on bare crooked trees** on a stony ridge from July to October: the kapok bush [ref:rfk-cochlospermum].
- **Kapok drifting** and split capsules under the tree in the late dry [ref:rfk-bombax] [ref:rfk-cochlospermum].
- **Conical spines** on a straight young trunk [ref:wiki-bombax].
- **A bee with a hum louder than a bee** has a streamer on it; see below [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Where they grow
sections.body: The cotton tree is a coastal tree: monsoon forest and river banks from sea level to 300 m on the Peninsula and the north-east [ref:rfk-bombax]. The kapok bush takes the rocky open forest [ref:rfk-cochlospermum]; native cotton the sandy ground near the watercourses [ref:wiki-gossypium]; and Palmer's *Kurrutcha* grew 'on the banks of the Mitchell in good soil' [ref:palmer1883]. Each place below says which of them grows there.

sections.heading: The calendar tree
sections.body: The cotton tree flowers in the dry when it has no leaves, which is why it is such a clear signal: 'when it blooms (big red flowers) it signals the start of the scrub hen egg season', and the flame tree says the same thing [ref:hershberger1982] [ref:rfk-bombax]. The [seasons](entry:seasons) page puts the dictionary's flowering signs in order. Its nectar feeds the honeyeaters and lorikeets of a leafless forest; its leaves feed the aeroplane butterfly; its kapok carries the seed on the wind [ref:rfk-bombax]. As a canoe tree it stood beside the [red cedar](entry:red-cedar) and the [candlenut](entry:candlenut), soft, light, straight timbers that a [stone axe](entry:axes-and-adzes) could fell and fire could hollow [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Seasons
sections.body: Leafless and flowering in the dry; the kapok bush bare between July and October; capsules opening in the late dry; the egg season of the mound-builders, which the flowers announce, from September [ref:rfk-bombax] [ref:rfk-cochlospermum] [ref:hershberger1982]. Kapok-bush roots were dug 'in the wet season, when excavation is easier' [ref:rfk-cochlospermum]. Canoe timber was felled after the first storms with the other big timber work [ref:anderson1996]. See [the year on country](entry:seasons).

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
- **Canoe hulls** on the coast, and **bee-tracking** with a cotton streamer: see the eastern coast below.
- **A calendar.** The red flowering marks the scrub-hen egg season [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Kapok-bush roots** roasted: Palmer on the Mitchell, and the rainforest key's note that 'Aboriginal people dig up the roots of small plants of this species. They are baked in ashes and hammered to soften them before being consumed' [ref:palmer1883] [ref:rfk-cochlospermum].
- **Kapok.** In India and Nepal the fibre is carded, spun and stuffed into pillows; no Kuku Yalanji use of the fibre is on record [ref:wiki-bombax].

sections.heading: Using the cotton trees
sections.body:
**Kapok-bush roots** [ref:palmer1883] [ref:rfk-cochlospermum]: in the wet, when the ground is soft, dig the long thick roots of small young plants; roast them in the ashes until the skin peels; hammer them soft; the inside is 'white and delicate and well-flavoured'.

**A canoe** from a cotton tree is on the [canoes](entry:canoes) page [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
- Young cotton trees are armed with conical spines [ref:wiki-bombax].
- Roots are taken only from small young plants, which kills them; take a few [ref:rfk-cochlospermum].
- Kapok bushes differ from place to place, and Palmer's root may have been yet another plant by his description. The method is the same; the plant should be checked [ref:rfk-cochlospermum] [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body: The cotton tree still flowers on the coastal rivers every dry season and still says what it said: eggs [ref:rfk-bombax]. Gathering on native title country is protected by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* [ref:alrc].

sections.body: *[wawuburra](word:wawuburra)* 'cottontree'; *[bilar](word:bilar)* 'candle nut tree'; *[ngakun](word:ngakun)* 'flame tree; species of yam'; *[nganjirr](word:nganjirr)* 'grass tree'; *[nganyin](word:nganyin)* 'sugar bag'; *[dabu](word:dabu)*, *[kuja](word:kuja)* the bees [ref:hershberger1982].

locations.summary: On the Hann, the tree the Kuku Thaypan Elders call the **cotton tree** is the yellow-flowered kapok tree, *Cochlospermum gillivraei*, not the red *Bombax* of the coast [ref:standley2019]. The Atlas of Living Australia holds 8 records of it, from 1970 to 2021, in a box of about 90 × 85 km around the middle Hann, Laura and western Rinyirru, and only one unconfirmed *Bombax* (2024, not identified to species) [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: The cotton tree here
sections.body: In the Elders' words, recorded by Standley: 'This tree grows in sand ridges and rocky areas. It has a spectacular habitat and a bright yellow flower. When the fruits are forming and maturing the tree losses most of its leaves' [ref:standley2019]. No native cotton (*Gossypium australe*) is recorded in the Hann box; the only cotton records there are introduced cottons, from 1998–1999 [ref:ala-hann].

sections.heading: Its year here
sections.body: It flowers from **June to October**, through the dry, on bare branches [ref:standley2019]: yellow on the stony ridges when the country is brown.

sections.heading: How the people of this country used it
sections.body: **String.** The Kuku Thaypan Elders, whose country takes in the middle and lower Hann [ref:fca-thaypan], recorded that 'the bark of the tree was used to make string' [ref:standley2019]. Their table gives no language name for it. Eating the roots of the kapok bush is recorded elsewhere (see the general sections), but not for this country.

locations.summary: At [Karma Waters](place:karma-waters) the cotton tree itself is not in the records; what is there is its cousins: the kapok bush *Cochlospermum*, which flowers yellow on the bare rocky ridges in the dry, and the native cotton *Gossypium australe*, recorded on the sandy ground near the watercourses [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:rfk-cochlospermum] [ref:wiki-gossypium]. Its roots are a wet-season food that Palmer recorded on the Mitchell in 1883 [ref:rfk-cochlospermum] [ref:palmer1883].

sections.heading: Which ones grow here
sections.body: The one recorded within 30 km of Karma Waters is *Cochlospermum gregorii*, the kapok bush of the dry northern savanna, the same kind of plant [ref:ala-karma-plants].

sections.heading: Safety here
sections.body:
- The kapok bush of the key and the one near Karma Waters are two species; Palmer's root was a third plant by his description. The method is the same; the plant should be checked [ref:rfk-cochlospermum] [ref:ala-karma-plants] [ref:palmer1883].
- Felling on the station is a matter for the lessee's permission [ref:kw-about].

sections.heading: On country today
sections.body: Gathering on native title country is protected by section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993*, as recognised for Western Yalanji country [ref:alrc] [ref:wyac2020].

locations.summary: On the Bloomfield it was one of the three favourite hulls for the [outrigger canoe](entry:canoes), and on the Endeavour River Roth found the same tree in the dug-outs [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1910]. The bush cotton had one more use at Bloomfield: tied as a streamer to a bee, it hummed loudly enough to follow to the hive [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: How people used it here
sections.body:
- **Canoe hulls.** 'A "cotton tree" (probably *Bombax malabaricum*)' was among the three timbers 'most favoured on the Bloomfield coast' for the dug-out; Roth found *Bombax* hulls on the Endeavour [ref:anderson1996] [ref:roth1910].
- **Bee-tracking.** 'Idriess describes how Aborigines at China Camp attached a "streamer" of bush cotton to a bee's body. This streamer made a loud hum as the bee flew and it was easy to then track it to the hive' [ref:anderson1996].

sections.heading: Following a bee with a streamer
sections.body:
From Idriess, at China Camp on the Bloomfield [ref:anderson1996]:

1. Catch a sugarbag bee at a flower or a water-hole.
2. Tie a wisp of bush cotton, kapok or native-cotton lint, to its body.
3. Let it go; the streamer 'made a loud hum as the bee flew', and it flies home.
4. Follow the hum to the tree, then see [native bees](entry:native-bees) for getting the sugarbag out.
